projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Stanley Ogrizek was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.p: That just about covers everything I was seeing ya know but, but history-

sp.p: Okay this-

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: This is a- I'm Renee Ogrizek, and I'm interviewing Stan J. Ogrizek. Today's date is October 10,2008, and we're located at Stanley's house in Akron, Ohio. He was in the first infantry division in World War two between the years of 1941 and 1946. Um what was- His date of birth is May 11, 1911, (background talking) His place ofbirth is Akron, Ohio. Where?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Place of birth? It was Cleveland, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Cleveland, Ohio is the place of birth.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Where we you raised as a child?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well a little bit of everything I mean from Cleveland, West Virginia, Barberton. Most of my life was spentin Barberton and- Akron.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Ok. And was your mother a first generation flum another country?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What country?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Yugoslavia.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Ok. What year was she born?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: (laughs) I have a record of it somewhere in another box.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Ok. That's Ok. And was your father first generation?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Yugoslavia, too. They were both born from Yugoslavia. They came over here as immigrants ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Do you remember what year they came over?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Ok.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Um. Tell me about your earliest memory?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh earliest memory. There's so many of them it's kinda hard to dwell on it ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Um. Your earliest memory of a child?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well when I lived in the coal mines.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: You lived in the coal mines. What was that like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh that was in a- Some of the places- See- Do- Do- In the twenties when things got tough. The family movedwherever there was work ya know. Like everybody else did. Like they"re doing today ya know. You move where there"s work. And00- They- I had an experience- It" s- It" s a spiritual experience ya know it's kinda difficult to explain ya know. (cane and newspaper being suflled on the floor) I want to get this out of the way here. It's of a spiritual nature. It's kinda hard to explain it ya know. In the twenties, middle twenties when I was in my teens ya know. 1- I experienced something of a spiritual nature and ya know it stuck with me ever since. It was something mystical that I couldn't explain. That's before I even knew what a church was. I never knew what a church was until we moved to Barberton in the later- In the middle thirties yaknow. And 00- And I think I was- In myself I think I was protected all my life that way. I know it sounds odd ya know butthat's the truth. That's why I went through all them wars. You got a list of them there. A list of my battles.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh we put it away. It's ok. (papers shuflling)

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Here it is. These are all my battles that I was in- And Africa and in Sicily. And 000We was instrumental- We was- When we invaded Dran. It's a naval base. And 00- From there we went to other places. We go out to Africa. I was in the battle of Fied (??) Pass. I don't know if you've ever heard of Case me Pass.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: You heard of it. Well that's when the Germans pushed us all the way back. To the Caseme Pass- And that's where the Australians come to our rescue ya know. And Db- It kinda- There's so much that happened in between. We- Everything was censored. We were not allowed to carry any information or pictures with us ya know. That was a policy then but today ifs different. I think it might be limited ya know. And 00- They 00- But while I was in the service- Ever since I went over there I was classified as a technician. It's something that yaknow- And- And- As a- As a- I had gone to the first infantry. And they're classified today as Special Forces ya know. Thafs something different. YouuYou- First Infantry you don't hear muchabout them anymore because they- Thafs a different kind of situation ya know. And 00- They 00- When I collapsed in Sicily about the time that Patton slapped that kid ya know. I was in the same hospital the next day when Patton slapped that kid ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uhhuh.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Which I thought was wrong. When he was in the hospital you know.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Thatpart- I read that. I'll never forget that part. And a- After I spent a couple months in the hospital they couldn~t find nothing physically wrong. But ifs a- But whatever happened there I'm paying for it now ya know because it's something. It's the- The military just don't- There's a lot of things they just don't understand ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you feel when you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Drafted?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I was drafted I believe it was 1941 or something like that. Well I was one of them that was drafted for one year. And after I was in there for nine months then they declared war. Well you know how that happens when they declare war. That- You stay in for the duration. That was a policy then. Well the policy today is they don't have no draft today like they did then ya know. It's something different than what we experienced. And 00- They 00- And- And a- After I got out of the army. I worked for PPG industry as an electrician. I generally retired in eighty-three I think it was eighty-three. I retired from PPG.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your family feel about you being drafted?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well- Well it was difficult for a lot of people yaknow.It's not so bad being drafted but what's difficult for a lot of people when they- They become a casualty of war. And aaOur job- What we had- The infantry I was with the first infantry you don't hear much about it today because we did the kind of war where we infiltrated. We fought at night time. In Africa and Sicily we fought at night time. It's a little bit different then it is today ya know. And they're better equipped today too ya know. And fighting at nighttime is a little bit different then fighting in plain daylight ya know. And that's what we had to do.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How old were you when you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh I don't know how old I was. I was young for my age. No my twenty. When I was drafted I think it was 1941. I told you the day I was. It's on my record there.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uh huh. 1941.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Forty-one I was drafted. That's when they drafted you for one year. That was before the war started. See Iwas drafted before the war started. And then after- After I was in there nine months we declared war. And as- And when we declared war that means you're in for the duration.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uh huh. How did. What did you know about the war before you were drafted?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Not- Not much. It was my first time in there.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: I mean what did you know about what was going on in the world.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: There's a lot of things they don't tell you ya know. Because a- You had to be careful what you you said toanybody you know. You can't tell whose listening ya know or recording what. We always depended on the information that they received from sources ya know. And a-

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Do you remember your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What do you remember about your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you bad to get used to it ya know. You bad to get used to it I guess.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Um tell me about your training in boot camp you went through

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well we were. When we first went in we went to camp in Walters, Texas for basic training. And then after we bad our basic training by- By almost 9 months later we were transferred to Fort Dev~??) and- And we transferred in to the regular army. It was 15 men 15 men from the whole company that were drafted from the regular army. We were transferred from the regular army ya know. Regular- And a- That's where we stayed until everything got.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How were people treated differently based on their gender, race, or ethnicity.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Gender or race. We didn't have that then. They did when we first went in there. They separated the colored ya know. They had a separate unit of their own yaknow. Then later on they integrated. They mixed them together. Like they're doing today.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you handle the physical demands?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I bad. I was in pretty good shape at that time. Even today I'm not in too bad of a shape today except that I have a hip problem ya know and have difficulty walking and a. now I have to go for treatment this coming Tuesday I have to see my doctor again and a- It became difficult ya know to. But I was always physically. Even in my work I mean when they need somebody that bad to do the climbing. Ya know. Utility poles and stuff like that. There was probably only a handful that could do it. Ya know or they didn't care to do it. Ya know. That's the way to put it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Vb huh. What were yourinstrnctors like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Huh.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were your instructors like in the service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Instructions?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Instructors. Um the people that trained you. What were they like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh they weren't too bad.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was the first place you went to in World War two?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: First place when the Whenthe War started. When the war started I was in a stage (??) I forgot to tell youwhen I got transferred to the first infantry. Our (??) general. Well guess who he was. He was he was a son of a former president. Teddy Roosevelt. That made a difference.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Vb huh. How did that affect you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. Well he fought in world war one and then when- When he joined us he- He was a whole man already. (laughs) we was almost twice as young as he was. He was older then we were ya know. I remember. That part I remember. I think I got a picture of him. (opening a container)

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh its okay we can get that afterward.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I think I had some pictures of him.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How were you welcomed by the people in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. I thought I bad some pictures. (looking in container for pictures) let me find then. Oh here's a bunch of them.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Stanley how were you welcomed by the people in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh not bad as long as we behaved ourselves ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were some of your biggest cultural differences?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well we couldn't understand their language yaw know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were the first days like you spent there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were the first days like that you spent in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: First-

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Couple first days.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: First days?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. See this guy here that's sitting down. (showing a picture) he was geneml teddy Roosevelt. General teddy Roosevelt right here. And this is our major here. And- And part of the time I was a radio operator. And- And in the infantry.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was yourjob in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you know what you're supposed to do with a gun don't ya.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uh huh. Um what was the desert war like and the battles you were in- In North Africa.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well they were a- Let me see I want to put this in here. (putting a picture away) what wasthat?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were the battles like in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well kinda hard to describe it with everything happened at night time yaknow.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Um what were? What was it like fighting along with the British?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: With the British. They were good ya know. And we fought in Africa we fought with the French foreign legion. I don't know if you've ever heard of them or not. But afterward we captured the naval base of Or an. That's when the foreign legion they give up because the Germans were in Africaya know. When they gave up they joined us in the fighting and for the duration of the war we fought with the foreign legion ya know. That's something you don't hear much about. And the foreign legion they're the ones that fought in Vietnam before Vietnam fell ya know. That's when Nixon was president ya know. And a- That's where they evacuated it was just too much for them. Vietnam and after Vietnam then we went in there and we got beat back.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was your most memorable experience in North Africa in world war two?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: And there's so many of them you can't remember all of them ya know

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was your favorite one?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well the old favorite one was when we could go back and pick up our wounded ya know the next morning and right under their noses in the daylight hours. I still remember that. They would allow us- if we left our weapons behind and under their noses we could pickup our wounded ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uh huh but-

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Which isunusoal ya know. They could have killed us if they wanted to. Qaughs) but they didn't And then Rommel, he was my favorite general. He was a German general ya know. Him and Hitler disagreed ya know. He never __ (??) Hitler would've listened to him ya know but Hitler liked to have his way ya know. And Hitler had him- had to get rid of him ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Why was he your favorite general?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: He was sympathetic. He was a- He was more of a- He was more of a- Everybody looked up to him ya know. He wasn't like the rest of them ya know. If it would've been the Japanese they would've shot all ofus ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you feel about Hitler?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I didn~t care too much for Hitler. You couldn't tell what he was thinking yaknow. And a- That was the bad part.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What tactics did you use in the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What tactics?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uh huh. Like how were the battles fought.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: It was fought with a rifle. That's what we had. We didn't have no body armor like they do today because we had to move fast at night time yaknow. And filtrate. We spent a lot of time behind enemy lines which they don't do today ya know. It's kinda hard to infiltrate today.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were the conditions like for the soldiers?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Not- I wouldn't say they was too bad, not for us anyhow. As long as we had something to eat ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What kind of food did you eat?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What kind of food did you eat?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well regular food that they made ya know. At night time- At night time they would eat not in the day time.Renee Ogrizek:: What did you do during the day time?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: We just rested (??)

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you feel about the victory in North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well towards the end Igot kinda used to it ya know. It's kinda hard to understand that ya know. But it didn't matter anymore ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Where did you travel to when you left North Africa?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: When we left North Africa we went to a Staten Island. Staten Island. There's a hospital in Staten Island. And it's on the record. (papers shuflling) on Staten Island.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you do in Staten Island?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well we stayed there for a physical and stuff like that ya know? Then we was transferred to __ (11) to West Virginia in a military hospital and it was a green brian (11) hotel at that time. __ (11) And- They a- We was there for two months. And after two months they couldn't find nothing physically wrong and so they just- They limited our service ya know to the United States.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: When did you travel to Sicily?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: It's on there.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: After you left North Africa you went to Sicily.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Yeah. It tells you all that doesn't it.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I think: I got it on there. Don~t I have it on there?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Vb huh. What happened in Sicily when you got there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well that's something difficult to talk: to you know. When they invaded Sicily- We invaded Sicily and when- Everybody knew that our a- That~s a story that I have. Everybody knew that we was supposed to get aid from Tunisia ya know. They fought the war at night time. They made sure that everybody understood that. So then during the night time the Germans invaded the harbor and burned up a couple of our ships and aaThey a- They got tangled up in our navy. Our navy was bombarding the people that were a bombarding our ships ya know. And a- They a- They a- That~s something that Patton knew- Patton knew that it wasn~t safe for them to come over. And Patton says the order stands ya know. He wasn~t going to change his mind. So when they come down we lost 600 paratroopers and there was- I thought it was unnecessary. That~s something that they don't talk about in the history books. About the 600 paratroopers. Most of them perished yaknow. Because our navy shot them down. They were doing their job. What they were supposed to do ya know. Cause the Germans were attacking the harbor. It was a difficult situation. And I've got some history books here and they don~t have what I'm talking about.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did that make you feel?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. After that- When them guys landed. What few that landed in Sicily. It was airborne. They a- They a-They a- (??) Some of them guys that landed they a come towards us and we told them what way we was supposed to go and I know what they were looking for but Patton was no where on the island. No where. They was looking for a Patton. You know what would~ve happened- I hate to think what would~ve happened if Patton would~ve been on that island that night. He wouldn~t be alive long. That was his snap fool- He shou1dn~t have let the paratroopers come in from Tunisia. They was supposed to come infrom Tunisia at about one or two o'clock in the moming.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was um- what was the goal of the operation in um Sicily?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh that's when we was supposed to establish a beach head so the rest of the tanks and troops could land and go to northern Sicily. The Germans at that time expected us to land on northern Sicily but we landed on southern Sicily. That~s what led to the confusion.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: When were you most scared?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Scared? (laughs) well it's hard to say.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Vb huh. Do you remember a time? Do you remember a specific time?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: No. we kept no records of what we did. We weren't allowed to have any records. In case you got captured all you had was your name and serial number. That's all you needed. That's all you got. You weren't even allowed to have a camera. You're not supposed to carry no personal records even your personal identification that you bad on you. You weren't allowed to have it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: When did you think: you might die?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: When I might die? I figured it didn't matter.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well even today it doesn't matter because when your time comes that's it ya know. That's a reasoning you have to have.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What role did your religious beliefs play in your daily life during the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I was a catholic.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your religious beliefs change during the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well they didn't change no much. It was reinforced more than ever ya know. Because the more I thought about it and all the situations I was in I think: the Lord was on my side. Because I went all the way to and come back and I didn't even have a scratch on me but I had a lot of scrapple. It tore up my clothes and stuff like that. I bad a lot of close calls.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you do when you weren't battling?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well we were supposed to __ (??) like you~re supposed to do. Anybody that we could capture we captured them ya know. Otherwise- That's something that I've never believed in ya know. Killing people- That's something I never believed in ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Was it difficult to fight in the war since you didn't believe in that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well it's one of those things ya know. It's one of those- You got the gun and when it comes time they say- It's useless- They gave them-

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you do when you weren't in battle?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you know how it is. Make as much ground as you could during the day ya know. While you had the chanceya know. Because our goal was to get to Mecina (??). That's what separates Africa from Sicily ya know. And Germans evacuated. That was our goal. And that was the end of it for us ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Did you do any traveling while you were in Sicily?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: No. you ain't got no time to travel. They didn't give you that much time. You come over there to capture Sicily. That was your goal.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you learn while you were stationed there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you learn while you were stationed there?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: When I was stationed there. I wasn't stationed no where.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: When you were in Sicily what did you learn?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What did I learn?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: It didn't matter anymore ya know. You have to make up your mind that's it ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Why didn't it matter to you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you can't live forever. Just like today ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Did you play any pranks. What pranks did you play or what did you do for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: We didn't have no entertainment. They only thing that we had- The only entertainment we had was when the guys bad pay days and play with the dice ya -know. Gamble their money. Gamble their monthly wages ya know. That was our entertainment.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your superiors treat you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh they were pretty good. You could tell who tbe bad ones were and who the good ones were ya know. You could tell.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What were the good ones like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well they were more down to earth. They were more understanding. The younger officers that would come in there they would- They had a different view of what they're supposed to do ya know. It's difficult to be an officer during the war ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Uh huh. And what were the bad ones like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. Some of them were mean yaknow.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: In what ways were they mean?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. They had you go into battle sometimes when it was unnecessary. Stufflike that ya know. If they want to get rid of somebody they'd put them in a unit and keep them fighting until they got rid of them ya know. That's the way that works.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What- How did you feel when you knew you were going home?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Felt pretty good. When I come over here to New York harbor to Staten Island everything looked so different you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you do the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What did I do? I don't remember what I did.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your family greet you?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your family greet you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh. Ok.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was your first memory after returning home?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: The first memory was eating something different than what the British fed us. The British fed us mutton and fisbya know. That was our mealya know. And when you get down to it mutton- They tried to give us mutton when we come to Staten Island and I could tell by looking at it- It was mutton and I didn't care for it. Mutton is sheep ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was the first meal that you ate? What was the first meal that you ate when you came home?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: staten Island.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was the food that you-

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I don't remember what food it was. It wasn't mutton. We had vegetables and stuff that we could eat ya know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What had changed when you returned home?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What has changed? Well. That's a difficult question to ask. You know today there's so many changes occurring today that the people can't get used to it ya know. They can't understand. It's like when I listen to- I listen to the radio quite a bit and a lot of people just don't understand the economics. If they understood economics we wouldn't be in the situation we had today. But today you have so many people that are greedy, they're deceitful, they lie to ya stuff like that ya know. It just isn't right 13 know. All they care about is more money and more money don't solve their problems.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did the people feel about the war in America?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well like they do today. I mean I don't know if there's- I have no way of knowing.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How were you treated?-

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: 1- 1- As far as I'm concerned I can't- Even when I left Sicily they asked me ifl knew what I was fighting for. You know what I told them. I says in about three or four years in combat I said I still don't know what I was fighting for. That was the truth.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How were you treated as a veteran?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you were treated different when you were in there you know but- Things change you know. Just like today. How- What are you doing today to make things better for ya. I hear that on the radio all the time and have all kinds of arguments. What they would do 13 know the candidates would do this or do that. What's better for ya. Everybody's got their opinion. When ya got a hundred people, a thousand people got different opinions you ain't gonna get no where. They have to agree on something. That's the problem today.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was your opinion?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was your opinion?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: My opinion. Today do the best I can with what you have you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What are you most proud of from your war service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh a lot of the memories you know that you have. That you could exchange. There wasn't too much of it you know but a lot of people don't believe you anyhow. They don't want to listen to it. A lot of people they don't want to listen to your war experience. They don't wantto.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was your favorite memory?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. That you're free. 1bat you can do what you want to do. 1bat's the way it works. It's up to you. Theyain't gonna do it for you, you have to do it for yourself.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What are you least proud of in your war service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. Things coukrve been better but they weren't. They could've been better but they weren't. Too many people had different opinions and that don't work.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you dislike most about the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: The fighting.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you feel about the fighting?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well that's difficult to answer you know. Most of my time was spent capturing at night time. Prisoners youknow. Most of it at night you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you do with the prisoners?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you do with the prisoners?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: 1- 1- What?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What didyou do with the people that you captured?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well we rounded them up and turned them in. They were prisoners you know. And I don't know where they took them. I mean why should they kill them you know. That's the way I looked at it. They want to live to you know. Boy you got a lot of questions to answer here.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your war experience affect you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: My weapons?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did your war experience affect you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well it wasn't too good.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What happened?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I didn't care for the fighting. I saw no reason for fighting. Well it's just like today. Everybody wants to fight this and fight that. If you want to fight I'll get out of your way and you go in there and do the fighting. That's the way I look at it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: In what ways was your life changed after the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I didn't say too much. There's no sense in me preaching to people if they don't want to understand. It's difficult- If you haven't been in there it's difficult to understand.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you wish people could have understood?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well then we go back to the first question. Just like today how do you know what's going to happen to our economy next week. Do you listen to it?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What did you get out of it?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Um. Just that anything could happen.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Yeah well what are you talking about anything because a lot of things could happen. The people have to work together to make things work. You can't go out there and have ten different people do ten different things. You have to follow what's recommended you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about war in general?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about war in general?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I don't believe in it. I don't believe in that and I don't believe in a lot of things I don't believe in but sometimes you get into a situation where you're forced to do it you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you feel about being forced into it?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I didn't believe in it At first it was difIerent but after you was in there for awhile like I told you before I don't know why we went over there in the first place. And there was such a big disagreement between Hitler and all them other guys. How could you cope with stuff like that? You can't do it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you feel about harry Truman's decision to drop the atomic bomb to end the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I didn't- I didn't believe in it. Look how many people he killed.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about the people that were killed by the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I feel for them. I mean what can they do you know. It wasn't my doing.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How would you feel today if they brought back the draft?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I wouldn't feel so good about it. No. That's the worst thing you can do. I believe in a volunteer anny and treat them like volunteers you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How- How did you feel when the Korean War and the gulf war were happening?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Korea and what war?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: The gulfwar.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Korean War.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Vb huh. How did you feel during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well that's something- I never give it any thought you know. I wasn't involved in it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What do you think about war today?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well that goes back to the first question. I don't care for it. I told you many times I don't care for it.Renee Ogrizek:: What's your opinion on the current war happening in Iraq?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you have different opinions on it you know. One guy says one thing another guy says one thing but a lot of people just don't understand what's necessary. Everybody wants to fight a war but they don't want to go in and do the fighting. That's tbe problem.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What do you think is necessary?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. It's not my opinion.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What is your opinion?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. Ijust don't believe in it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What advice would you give a young person wanting to serve today?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: WelL You have to make your own judgment you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about if your family was involved in the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I'd feel a little bit different you know. My brother was in the war but he ain't living today. He died of a stroke about seven, eight years ago. He was in the coast guard you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about German and Japanese people today'?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well it ain't the people it's the leaders that you have to contend with.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about the leaders?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well some of the leaders we got today I don't care too much for them. The leaders we used to have years ago. You don't have them anymore. We don't have that kind of people today.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What do you thinks changed between-

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. Everybody wants to be boss. They want to do it their way. That's the problem. Instead of getting together and agree on something they don't believe in that.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What would you change about war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you asked me that about ten times already. What would I change? Forget about the war. That's the only thing I would- Today they're talking about diplomacy you know. Why don't we have good diplomats? We don't have any.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you think a fair argument or war should be resolved?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well diplomacy. That's it. That's what they're trying to do now.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was the aftermath of war like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was the aftermath of the war like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Aftermath. You asked me that about ten times already. After the war- I mean theeThat part I don't care about it you know. The aftermath. When I'm not in there it don't matter.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about war protestors?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well if they know what they're doing it's different but you got a lot of protestors but that's all they're doing protesting causing trouble you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How do you feel about people that criticize the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well that's their business. If you have a good reason for it that's different but if you don't have a good reason for it that's something else.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What would be a good reason to criticize the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well what people have to understand today with what's going on in the world todayyYou'd be surprised. I listen to the radio. You turned it off. What's so much comes up there everybody has a different opinion. What are you doing to do when you have thousands of people that have different opinions? What can you do you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What would you do?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Me. I wouldn~t do nothing. I'djust stand by and listen. I mean-

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What is a normal day like for you today?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well today. Normal days- Keeping alive you know. I have a hip problem. And Tuesday I have to go see the doctor again. I had a MIR. Let's see- Last Tuesday I had a MIR. This coming Tuesday I'm going to have the doctor examine me again. My biggest goal today is to take care of my hip. Find out what the problem is. That's my goal. Just like everybody else's goal. If it wasn't for my hip I could do more.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How often do you think about your service?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Not very much. I don't care for it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How does it make you feel?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How does it make you feel about being in the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you asked me that about four or five times already. I don't care for it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What would you want to forget about your experience?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Forget about all of it I mean. I just- If you had a good reason for it- It would be different but if you don't have a good reason for it forget about it.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Have you talked to anybody else about your experience?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: No. I don't think they care to hear it. I don't think they care to hear about it. My next thing I got to do I got to take some Metamucil. I got to take that everyday for my bowel movement. Metamucil you know. That has to go and I got to eat. That's my problem today.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Is there anything else you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: No I ain't got nothing to add.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How- How would you feel if your grandchild was in the war?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: My grandfather?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Grandchild-

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Grandchild- I wouldn't feel too good. I know how I'd feel because my granddaughter's husband was in the Special Forces. He died in Iraq. And it didn't make me feel too good.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did it affect your family?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. He was a career soldier. That's what he was. Special Forces career.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did you help your granddaughter through that time?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I'm helping her out now with all I can you know. What can I do? My granddaughter's a school teacher you know and they're making it{)k you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did losing people make you feel?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Meeting people?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Losing people in the war.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well you get used to it. I've seen thousands of them die in the war myself and you get used to it. It's nothing new you know. When somebody dies or gets wounded or something we just leave them behind. The paramedics would take care of them and we would move on you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How would you feel ifit would've been you?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well that's one of those things you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Why do you think you're protected? Why do you think you're spiritually protected?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Why am I being protected? Well I always felt the Lord was on my side from the beginning like I told you back in the coal mines you know when I experience the spiritual up in the skies in the twenties, 1920s, and ever since that time I believed the Lord was on my side.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What was that spiritual experience like?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well it's hard to explain or put it in words.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: How did that make you feel by having that?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Just like today. How many people believe there is a God. A lot of people don't understand. They want something they can see you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What do you think about it today?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: About God.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I believe in God.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Do you still go to church?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I still go to church. In fact today I had a guy come over that wanted to give me communion you know. He wanted to give me communion every week. I said once a month is enough. I said I got other things that have to be done besides going to communion all the time you know. I ain't got that kind of time. I ain't got nobody out here but myself. When you're by yourself your situation is different. Somebody else can do all the things for you but if you're by yourself you got to do it. If! don't do it- It don't get done. That's the way it is.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Vb huh. How do you feel about Memorial Day and Veteran's Day?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well. Like always.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: What do you do to celebrate them?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I visit the memorial. I visited the graveyards you know.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Is there any particular grave that you visit?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Oh I visit my wife's grave. I usually visit my wife's grave.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Do you visit any veteran's graves?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Not that I know of. The cemetery is just full of veteran's graves on Memorial Day. You go on Memorial Day and there's flags all over the place. Except in my case it says I was a vet in world war two but when I pass away I'll have a flag on my grave too you know. There's a lot of veterans. On Memorial Day go to the graveyard. You'll see.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Did you join- What veteran organizations did you join?

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: I didn't join any. No veteran's organizations. They wanted me to go join the VFW down here. But I like to go down there and have lunch and that's about it. But it takes a lot of time to go to them organizations you know. It takes your time. When you got other things to do that have to be done: washing, take care of your food, make sure you eat or whatever's going to happen. If you don't do it- It don't get done. It don't get done if you don't do it. Period. A lot of people think that just because you're retired you ain't got nothing to do. A lot of people ask me that question but you're retired you ain't got nothing to do. Well you better wake up a little bit.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: Well thank you for your time.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: Well I did the best I could.

sp.speaker: Renee Ogrizek
sp.p: You did a good job.

sp.speaker: Stanley Ogrizek
sp.p: (laughs)
